cues.text: Nearly Sixty Years Unresolved
Since Italian troops seized Rome in 1870, ending papal temporal rule over the former Papal States, successive popes refused to recognize Italy’s sovereignty over the city.
They declined the unilateral Italian Law of Guarantees, considering themselves 'prisoners of the Vatican.'
The resulting standoff, the Roman Question , poisoned Church-state relations in Italy for decades.
Pius XI Seeks Reconciliation
Upon his election in 1922, Pope Pius XI signaled his eagerness to resolve the impasse.
Secret negotiations began in 1926 between Domenico Barone for the Italian government and Francesco Pacelli, brother of the future Pius XII, representing the Holy See.
Pius XI closely supervised the talks, insisting above all on unambiguous recognition of full papal sovereignty over whatever territory would be assigned to the Holy See, however small.
Signing the Pacts

On February 11, 1929 , at the Lateran Palace in Rome, Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Gasparri signed the agreements on behalf of Pius XI, and Prime Minister Benito Mussolini signed on behalf of King Victor Emmanuel III.
The Lateran Pacts consisted of three parts: a political treaty creating the sovereign Vatican City State ; a financial convention compensating the Holy See for its lost territories.
The third was a concordat regulating the position of the Catholic Church within Italian law and society.
Terms of the Settlement

The treaty recognized the pope's full and exclusive sovereignty over the newly created Vatican City, a territory of just over 100 acres, in exchange for the Holy See's formal recognition of the Kingdom of Italy with Rome as its capital.
The accompanying concordat made Catholicism the official religion of Italy, granted Church recognition to canonical marriages, and reintroduced religious instruction into Italian schools.
A Complicated Alliance

The agreement was concluded with Mussolini's Fascist government, a fact that has drawn ongoing historical scrutiny and debate over the motives on each side — genuine ecclesial reconciliation for Pius XI, political legitimacy for Mussolini's regime.
Tensions between the Vatican and the Fascist state over the education of youth and the scope of Catholic Action would resurface within just a few years of the treaty's signing.
Legacy
The Lateran Treaty definitively resolved the Roman Question and remains, in modified form (renegotiated in 1984), the legal basis for Vatican City's status.
It establishes the world's smallest sovereign state and serves as the seat of the Holy See's independence from any other government.

It established the framework under which the papacy has operated ever since — as a spiritual authority backed by a minimal but fully sovereign territorial base, rather than the extensive temporal kingdom the popes once ruled.
